entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 2 Na 2:1-13 . The Advance of the Destroying Forces against Nineveh, after It Was Used as God's Rod for a Time to Chastise His People: The Capture of That Lion's Dwelling, According to the Sure Word of Jehovah. 1. He that dasheth in pieces-- God's "battle axe," wherewith He "breaks in pieces" His enemies. Jr 51:20 applies the same Hebrew term to Nebuchadnezzar (compare Pr 25:18 ; Jr 50:23 , "the hammer of the whole earth"). Here the Medo-Babylonian army under Cyaxares and Nabopolassar, that destroyed Nineveh, is prophetically meant. before thy face-- before Nineveh. Openly, so that the work of God may be manifest. watch the way-- by which the foe will attack, so as to be ready to meet him. Ironical advice; equivalent to a prophecy, Thou shalt have need to use all possible means of defense; but use what thou wilt, all will be in vain. make thy loins strong-- The loins are the seat of strength; to gird them up is to prepare all one's strength for conflict ( Job 40:7 ). Also gird on thy sword ( 2Sa 20:8 ; 2Ki 4:29 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12835"/><div sID="gen23881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12835"/><hi type="bold">2. For the Lord hath turned away the excellency of Jacob--</hi>that is, the time for Nineveh's overthrow is ripe, because Jacob (Judah) and Israel (the ten tribes) have been sufficiently chastised. The Assyrian rod of chastisement, having done its work, is to be thrown into the fire. If God chastised Jacob and Israel with all their "excellency" (Jerusalem and the temple, which was their pre-eminent excellency above all nations in God's eyes, <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.87.2">87:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Am 6:8</reference>), how much more will He punish fatally Nineveh, an alien to Him, and idolatrous? Maurer, not so well, translates, "restores," or "will restore the excellency of Jacob."<div eID="gen23881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">emptiers--</hi>the Assyrian spoilers.<div eID="gen23882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have emptied them out--</hi>have spoiled the Israelites and Jews (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Ho 10:1</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.16">Psa 80:8-16</reference>, on "vine branches," as applied to Israel. <div eID="gen23883" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12836"/><div sID="gen23884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12836"/><hi type="bold">3. his mighty men--</hi>the Medo-Babylonian general's mighty men attacking Nineveh.<div eID="gen23884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made red--</hi>The ancients dyed their bull's-hide shields red, partly to strike terror into the enemy, chiefly lest the blood from wounds which they might receive should be perceived and give confidence to the foe [Calvin]. G. V. Smith conjectures that the reference is to the red reflection of the sun's rays from shields of bronze or copper, such as are found among the Assyrian remains.<div eID="gen23885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in scarlet--</hi>or crimson military tunics (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.28">Mt 27:28</reference>). Xenophon mentions that the Medes were fond of this color. The Lydians and Tyrians extracted the dye from a particular worm.<div eID="gen23886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chariots ... with flaming torches--</hi>that is, the chariots shall be like flaming torches, their wheels in lightning-like rapidity of rotation flashing light and striking sparks from the stones over which they pass (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.28">Is 5:28</reference>). English Version supposes a transposition of the Hebrew letters. It is better to translate the Hebrew as it is, "the chariots (shall be furnished) with fire-flashing scythes" (literally, "with the fire," or glitter, of iron weapons). Iron scythes were fixed at right angles to the axles and turned down, or parallel to it, inserted into the felly of the wheel. The Medes, perhaps, had such chariots, though no traces of them are found in Assyrian remains. On account of the latter fact, it may be better to translate, "the chariots (shall come) with the glitter of steel weapons" [Maurer and G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen23887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the day of his preparation--</hi>Jehovah's (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Is 13:3</reference>). Or, "Medo-Babylonian commander's day of preparation for the attack" (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Na 2:1</reference>). "He" confirms this, and "his" in this verse.<div eID="gen23888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fir trees--</hi>their fir-tree lances.<div eID="gen23889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terribly shaken--</hi>branded so as to strike terror. Or, "shall be tremulous with being brandished" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen23890" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12839"/><div sID="gen23901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12839"/><hi type="bold">6. The gates of the rivers ... opened--</hi>The river wall on the Tigris (the west defense of Nineveh) was 4,530 yards long. On the north, south, and east sides, there were large moats, capable of being easily filled with water from the Khosru. Traces of dams ("gates," or sluices) for regulating the supply are still visible, so that the whole city could be surrounded with a water barrier (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.8">Na 2:8</reference>). Besides, on the east, the weakest side, it was further protected by a lofty double rampart with a moat two hundred feet wide between its two parts, cut in the rocky ground. The moats or canals, flooded by the Ninevites before the siege to repel the foe, were made a dry bed to march into the city, by the foe turning the waters into a different channel: as Cyrus did in the siege of Babylon [Maurer]. In the earlier capture of Nineveh by Arbaces the Mede, and Belesis the Babylonian, Diodorus Siculus, [1.2.80], states that there was an old prophecy that it should not be taken till the river became its enemy; so in the third year of the siege, the river by a flood broke down the walls twenty furlongs, and the king thereupon burnt himself and his palace and all his concubines and wealth together, and the enemy entered by the breach in the wall. Fire and water were doubtless the means of the second destruction here foretold, as of the first.<div eID="gen23901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dissolved--</hi>by the inundation [Henderson]. Or, those in the palace shall melt with fear, namely, the king and his nobles [Grotius]. <div eID="gen23902" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12840"/><div sID="gen23903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12840"/><hi type="bold">7. Huzzab--</hi>the name of the queen of Nineveh, from a Hebrew root implying that she stood by the king (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>), [Vatablus]. Rather, Nineveh personified as a queen. She who had long stood in the most supreme prosperity. Similarly Calvin. Maurer makes it not a proper name, and translates, "It is established," or "determined" (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Ge 41:32</reference>). English Version is more supported by the parallelism.<div eID="gen23903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">led away captive--</hi>The Hebrew requires rather, "she is laid bare"; brought forth from the apartments where Eastern women remained secluded, and is stripped of her ornamental attire. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Is 47:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">3</reference>, where the same image of a woman with face and legs exposed is used of a city captive and dismantled (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>), [Maurer].<div eID="gen23904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought up--</hi>Her people shall be made to go up to Babylon. Compare the use of "go up" for moving from a place in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>.<div eID="gen23905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her maids ... as ... doves--</hi>As Nineveh is compared to a queen dethroned and dishonored, so she has here assigned to her in the image handmaids attending her with dove-like plaints (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Is 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">59:11</reference>. The image implies helplessness and grief suppressed, but at times breaking out). The minor cities and dependencies of Nineveh may be meant, or her captive women [Jerome]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12843"/><div sID="gen23914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12843"/>10. Literally, "emptiness, and emptiedness, and devastation." The accumulation of substantives without a verb (as in <reference osisRef="Nah.3.2">Na 3:2</reference>), the two first of the three being derivatives of the same root, and like in sound, and the number of syllables in them increasing in a kind of climax, intensify the gloomy effectiveness of the expression. Hebrew, Bukah, Mebukah, Mebullakah (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Is 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.4">3, 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.15">Zep 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faces of all gather blackness--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Joel.2.6">Joe 2:6</reference>). Calvin translates, "withdraw (literally, 'gather up') their glow," or flush, that is, grow pale. This is probably the better rendering. So Maurer. <div eID="gen23915" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12844"/><div sID="gen23916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12844"/><hi type="bold">11. dwelling of ... lions--</hi>Nineveh, the seat of empire of the rapacious and destructive warriors of various ranks, typified by the "lions," "young lions," "old lion" (or lioness [Maurer]), "the lion's whelp." The image is peculiarly appropriate, as lions of every form, winged, and sometimes with the head of a man, are frequent in the Assyrian sepulchres. It was as full of spoils of all nations as a lion's den is of remains of its prey. The question, "Where," &c., implies that Jehovah "would make an utter end of the place," so that its very site could not be found (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Na 1:8</reference>). It is a question expressing wonder, so incredible did it then seem. <div eID="gen23916" type="x-p"/>
